procedural_history.originating_court: Orders of detention were issued under Section 3(2) of the Preventive Detention Act IV of 1950.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of detention and subsequent confirmation orders under Section 11 of the Preventive Detention Act IV of 1950.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The text does not mention any High Court proceedings. The petitioners directly approached the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution of India.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioners challenged the legality of their detention in the Supreme Court, arguing that the State Government did not consider their representations against the detention orders but merely forwarded them to the Advisory Board. The Supreme Court held the detention orders against the petitioners illegal and ultra vires.

directions: the petitioners were consequently entitled to be released

issue.issue_text: Whether the constitution of an Advisory Board under Section 8 of the Act relieves the State Government from the legal obligation to consider the representation of the detenu.

facts: Petitioners were detained under the Preventive Detention Act and made representations to the State Government against their detention.
The State Government did not consider these representations itself but instead forwarded them to the Advisory Board.
The State Government argued that it had no obligation to consider the representations because an Advisory Board had been constituted for that purpose.
law: Article 22(5) of the Constitution guarantees a detenu the right to make a representation against their detention.
The Preventive Detention Act establishes an Advisory Board to report on whether a person should be detained for more than three months.
application: The Court found that the right to make a representation under Article 22(5) carries a "necessary implication" that the authority to whom it is made (the State Government) must consider it.

The Court distinguished between the roles of the State Government and the Advisory Board. The government's duty is to consider if the person should be detained at all, even for a single day, while the Board's role is to advise on detention beyond three months.

This right to have the representation considered by the government is guaranteed "independent of the duration of the period of detention and irrespective of the existence or non-existence of an Advisory Board."
Therefore, the government is under a legal obligation to consider the representation as expeditiously as possible and *before* referring the case to the Advisory Board.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the government's argument, holding that the constitution of an Advisory Board does not relieve the State Government from its separate and prior legal obligation to consider the detenu's representation.

issue.issue_text: Whether the State Government is only obliged to consider the representation of a detenu in a case where the detention is for a period of less than three months.

facts: The State Government contended that it was only obliged to consider a detenu's representation in cases where the detention was for less than three months.
For detentions longer than three months, the State argued that the review by an Advisory Board was sufficient, and the government itself did not need to consider the representation.
law: The Court centered its analysis on Article 22(5) of the Constitution, which guarantees a detenu the right to be informed of the grounds for detention and the earliest opportunity to make a representation against the detention order to the appropriate government.
application: The Court found that the right to make a representation under Article 22(5) is a fundamental constitutional right that is "guaranteed independent of the duration of the period of detention and irrespective of the existence or non-existence of an Advisory Board."
It rejected the State's attempt to create a "dichotomy" between two classes of detenus (those detained for less or more than three months), stating that the right applies equally to all.
The Court reasoned that it is a "necessary implication" of Article 22(5) that the State Government, to whom the representation is made, must personally consider it as expeditiously as possible.

It clarified that the role of the Advisory Board is distinct from the State Government's obligation. The government must consider whether a person should be detained "even for a single day," which is a separate and earlier duty than the Board's function of reviewing detentions that extend beyond three months.

Therefore, the constitution of an Advisory Board does not relieve the State Government of its legal obligation to consider the representation. In fact, the government must consider it *before* referring the case to the Board.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the State Government's argument, holding that the government is under a constitutional obligation to consider a detenu's representation in all cases, regardless of the length of detention or the involvement of an Advisory Board.

issue.issue_text: Whether Article 22(5) of the Constitution requires the State Government to consider the representations of the detenus, even in the absence of express language to that effect.

facts: Petitioners were detained under the Preventive Detention Act.
They made representations to the State Government against their detention.
The State Government did not consider these representations but instead forwarded them to an Advisory Board.

The State argued it had no obligation to consider the representations because Article 22(5) of the Constitution does not contain express language requiring it to do so, and because the Advisory Board's role is to consider the cases.
law: Article 22(5) of the Constitution guarantees a person detained under a law of preventive detention the right to be informed of the grounds for their detention and the right to make a representation against the order.
application: The Court rejected the State's argument that the absence of express language in Article 22(5) meant there was no obligation to consider the representation.
It held that it is a "necessary implication" of the language in Article 22(5) that the State Government must consider the representation as soon as it is made.
The Court reasoned that the constitutional right to make a representation would be rendered "illusory" and "nugatory" if the authority to whom it is made has no legal obligation to consider it.

The Court distinguished between the role of the State Government and the Advisory Board. The government's obligation is to consider whether a person should be detained "even for a single day," which is a separate and distinct duty from the Advisory Board's function of reporting on whether detention for more than three months is justified.
Therefore, the constitution of an Advisory Board does not relieve the State Government of its own legal obligation to consider the representation first.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the petitioner's argument, holding that it is necessarily implicit in Article 22(5) that the State Government has a legal obligation to properly and expeditiously consider a detenu's representation, even before forwarding it to an Advisory Board.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the constitution of an Advisory Board under Section 8 of the Act relieves the State Government from the legal obligation to consider the representation of the detenu.
appellant_arguments: The detention was illegal because there was a failure on the part of the Government to consider the representations submitted by the petitioners before forwarding them to the Advisory Board.
respondent_arguments: There was no obligation on the State Government to consider the representations since the Advisory Board had been constituted under Section 8 of the Act to consider the cases of the detenus.
To secure an unprejudiced and impartial consideration of the representation by the Advisory Board, the State Government refrained from expressing its views on the representations at that stage.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the State Government is only obliged to consider the representation of a detenu in a case where the detention is for a period of less than three months.
appellant_arguments: The government has a legal obligation to consider the representation in all cases, and the failure to do so renders the detention illegal (implied argument against the respondent's limited concession).
respondent_arguments: The State Government might be obliged to consider the representation of a detenu only in a case where the detention was for a period of less than three months, but not in a case where a reference has to be made to the Advisory Board.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Article 22(5) of the Constitution requires the State Government to consider the representations of the detenus, even in the absence of express language to that effect.
appellant_arguments: The government's failure to consider the representations made the detention illegal, implying that the obligation to consider them is a constitutional requirement under Article 22(5).
respondent_arguments: There was no express language in Article 22(5) of the Constitution requiring the State Government to consider the representations of the detenus.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The constitutional right of representation conferred by Article 22(5) on a person detained under a preventive detention law does not depend upon the duration of the period of detention. This right exists even if the period of detention is for less than three months.
obiter: Under Article 22(4) of the Constitution, Parliament can enact a law providing for preventive detention for a period of less than three months without the case being reviewed by an Advisory Board.
Under Article 22(7), Parliament may by law prescribe the circumstances under which and the class or classes of cases in which a person may be detained.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The constitutional right of a detenu to make a representation under Article 22(5) imposes a corresponding and independent legal obligation on the detaining authority to consider that representation. This duty is not relieved by the constitution of an Advisory Board to review the case, nor is it limited to detentions of a specific duration. Failure by the government to consider the representation is a breach of a fundamental procedural requirement that renders the detention illegal.
legal_tests_applied: The right of representation conferred by clause (5) of Art. 22 does not depend upon the duration of the period of detention.

The court uses a structural interpretation of the Constitution, reasoning that since the obligation to consider a representation would exist even under a law passed pursuant to Art. 22(7) (which allows for detention beyond three months without an Advisory Board), the obligation must be a fundamental requirement of Art. 22(5) itself, independent of any Board's existence.

In preventive detention cases, strict adherence to procedural requirements is mandatory, and if "one of the procedural requirement is not complied with, the order of detention would be rendered illegal."
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning reflects a policy of strictly interpreting laws that impinge on personal liberty. The requirement for the detaining authority to independently consider a representation is treated as a crucial procedural safeguard against arbitrary executive action, ensuring the authority applies its mind at the earliest opportunity.
